items.title: Taika Waititi Says His Star Wars Movie Is 'on Ice'
items.excerpt: Director Taika Waititi has confirmed his long-in-development Star Wars movie is officially "on ice."
items.content_text: Director Taika Waititi has confirmed his long-in-development Star Wars movie is officially "on ice." The Thor: Ragnarok and Jojo Rabbit filmmaker provided Inverse with the update when speaking to the outlet during a press junket for his new film, Klara and the Sun . When asked directly for the state of his and writer Tony McNamara's progress in the Star Wars universe, Waititi had a blunt answer. "I hate to break this to you, but we're going to actually put it on ice and we're working on a different thing together," he said. Brutal. Rumors that Disney and Lucasfilm had approached the What We Do in the Shadows filmmaker to helm a Star Wars project go as far back as January 2020. That's just a few years after he took off as the mastermind behind one of the most beloved Marvel Cinematic Universe movies to date, with an official announcement confirming he was attached to a movie arriving just a few months later. It was mostly good news at first. In 2021, Waititi said he had finished his Star Wars movie's story , and in 2022, then-Lucasfilm president Kathleen Kennedy said the goal was to bring it to theaters in late 2023 . At the time, she also admitted that Disney hadn't "locked anything in" quite yet, a fact that only became more apparent in the years that followed. Waititi was said to be "still working away" on the project on the third anniversary of its announcement in April 2023. After admitting he planned to prioritize other projects later that year, updates went mostly quiet. Waititi finally returned earlier this year to promise that his Star Wars movie was going to "harness a little bit more of the fun from the original trilogy." Now, it's all on ice. "Well, there's your answer," he continued during his conversation with Inverse. "I don't even know how to dress it up or make it even vague. It's very iced. I've got about four other movies I'm trying to do." It's years of updates that led to what will no doubt arrive as a disappointing announcement for many, even if it's not too surprising. Going on six years with little more than the occasional minor promise never spelled a bright future for Waititi's Star Wars. When Kennedy said she thought the project was "still somewhat alive" amid her Lucasfilm exit , fans started to expect the worst. None of this is to say Waititi hasn't stayed busy in the years between. In 2022, he launched Thor: Love and Thunder , with his Next Goal Wins movie then following the next year. Klara and the Sun will bring Jenna Ortega, Amy Adams, Steve Buscemi, and the rest of its all-star cast to theaters October 23, 2026, even if negative reviews have cast shade on its premiere. Early reception has landed it with a painful 23% on Rotten Tomatoes after 12 reviews so far. For now, it's unclear if his Star Wars movie will ever come to be. Even he sounded a bit unsure of what the future holds, adding, "Ice ages do come to an end. Who knows?" Photo by Stefania D'Alessandro/Getty Images.
items.title_en: Taika Waititi Says His Star Wars Movie Is 'on Ice'

items.title: Silent Hill Remake Studio Wants to Make Physical Games 'for as Long as Possible'
items.excerpt: Silent Hill developer Bloober Team wants to make physical versions of its games "for as long as possible."
items.content_text: Silent Hill developer Bloober Team wants to make physical versions of its games "for as long as possible." Studio CEO Piotr Babieno opened up about the company's appreciation for physical media and collectibles during an interview with GamesRadar . He started his thoughts by touching on how the gaming landscape and player desires have changed as technology has advanced over the years, explaining that "we have reached a moment where you can't really do much more" in terms of visual and auditory fidelity. "Like, OK, the game can have a slightly higher resolution and maybe better lighting and whatever, but will it make it a more engaging game? I don't think so," Babieno said. The CEO for the studio behind the Silent Hill 2 remake and its in-development original Silent Hill remake also talked about how stats show "the majority of players are playing on hardware which is five, seven years old, if not older." He continued, saying, "But are they less interested in games because of that? I don't think so." As AI shapes a new, controversial future in the gaming industry, the Bloober executive seems to be more interested in "thinking about other senses." It's this mindset that the team has carried into its new Nintendo Switch 2-exclusive 2.5D horror game, Onyx: The Dark Group . For this experience, which comes from Bloober subsidiary Broken Mirror Games, it's become about "putting horror back in your hands." "As humans, we have four other senses, and AI can deliver something for what you see, for what you hear, but why not touch?" Babieno said. "I think the physical element of gaming will always, always be there." When the conversation turned to the topic of physical games – which has become a hot-button issue in the wake of Sony's decision to kill disc releases for PlayStation games , as well as Rockstar's disc-less approach to Grand Theft Auto 6 – Babieno admitted he does see why some are beginning to favor digital releases. After all, as he said, "digital distribution is much easier, much cheaper, and will be more profitable for everyone." For Babieno, it's hard not to think about how game collecting has affected him, personally, when looking to the future . "Collecting games also [made] an emotional connection between the game and me, between the studio which produced the game and me," he said. "This little emotional touch is so important that, I think in some way, we would lose the opportunity of being closer with our fans [without it]. So, if we are able to produce a [physical] retail version of our games, we would like to make them for as long as possible." Also during the interview, Broken Mirror's executive director, Tymon Smektala, who left Dying Light developer Techland to join the Bloober company earlier this year, said that he and Babieno both share a love for game collecting. "Like, if I could unblur my screen, you would see lots of stuff behind me and I have lots of stuff that's not even in the camera, so this is what gaming is to us," he said during the video interview. "This is the gaming I know, and this is the gaming I expect. And as long as it will be possible, and as long as the big decision makers will allow us to have that, then of course I'll be into that." Bloober's Silent Hill 2 remake was initially released for PC and PlayStation 5 in 2024 and received physical disc support at the time. Supporting that angle for future games will officially become more complicated when Sony ends support for PlayStation discs in 2028. The Silent Hill 1 remake was announced in June of last year and currently remains without a release date. It's unclear if it will be out before Sony ends support on its end.
items.title_en: Silent Hill Remake Studio Wants to Make Physical Games 'for as Long as Possible'

items.title: Street Fighter Tops the Box Office With $51 Million Opening Weekend Amid Lackluster Reviews
items.excerpt: Capcom's Street Fighter movie spun up $51.1 million in its opening weekend, securing its place atop the global box office despite some not-so-great reviews.
items.content_text: Capcom's Street Fighter movie spun up $51.1 million in its opening weekend, securing its place atop the global box office despite some not-so-great reviews. Ryu (Andrew Koji), Ken (Noah Centineo), and the rest of the film's massive cast grappled with an estimated $31 million domestically and $20.1 million internationally in its theatrical debut. That's a figure that landed it a comfortable first place worldwide, even if it's not a perfect victory across the board. As audiences turned up for performances – including Callina Liang's Chun-Li, David Dastmalchian's M. Bison, and Jason Momoa's Blanka – not everyone was so happy with how director Kitao Sakurai brought Capcom's classic fighting game franchise to the big screen. In its first few days in the public's gaze, Street Fighter has amassed a critics' score of 44 on IMDb and 41% on Rotten Tomatoes . IGN gave it a 6/10 . That's serviceable as far as gaming adaptations go and sub-par in the grand scheme. Generally, fans are feeling pretty positive about what they've seen thanks to some crisp animation and fight sequences. " Dumb fun " is one phrase floating around for the film, which doesn't seem to be for everyone but has still pulled in 79% positivity from audiences, according to Rotten Tomatoes. For comparison (and because Street Fighter actor Andrew Schulz has it on everyone's minds ), the 2021 Mortal Kombat movie earned $22.5 million domestically in its post-lockdown-era debut . Mortal Kombat 2 , which continued that story earlier this year, opened to $63 million globally, coming in second place behind The Devil Wears Prada 2. That gives Mortal Kombat the edge over its Capcom competitor in terms of direct box office performance worldwide as the teams behind both projects tease ideas for a crossover . The real test for Street Fighter will be its performance in the weeks ahead. Paramount, Legendary, and Capcom made the adaptation with a production budget of $82 million, according to Deadline . We're not quite at that number yet, and if word of those bad reviews spreads too far, the video game movie's fight for a sequel might be more of an uphill battle than expected. While Street Fighter takes the top box office spot, also in theaters this weekend is Nathan Fielder's You Can See Everything . A mind-bending look into the life of controversial Theranos creator Elizabeth Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, the dark-comedy documentary has enraptured moviegoers with $15 million domestically. That's a number that puts it well below the wide appeal garnered by Street Fighter, but considering the three-hour Fielder doc opened to just 855 theaters compared to the video game movie's 3,575, it's hard not to see You Can See Everything as a more impressive success story. Its production budget reportedly totaled less than $10 million, with its marketing budget also said to be around that same number. Reviews for the movie are showing incredible positivity, too, with movie reviewer social media platform Letterboxd boasting that You Can See Everything quickly emerged as its highest-rated feature film. IGN's review returned a "Masterpiece" rating of 10/10 . We called it "a jaw-dropping, intimate investigative doc" that "finds TV host Nathan Fielder searching the deep-blue eyes of Silicon Valley scammer Elizabeth Holmes for mysterious answers." Fielder's latest is only available as a limited release for now. The plan is for it to get a much wider release in the near future, with one Deadline source saying, "Who knows where this will go." Elsewhere in theaters, moviegoers have had the opportunity to watch two Capcom adaptations as Resident Evil continues its successful run. While star Austin Abrams rides that wave of success, his other picture, Whalefall , which debuted this weekend, only managed to wash up $17.5 million on its $60 million budget. For more on Street Fighter, you can read why we think it makes a mistake that Mortal Kombat already learned from . You can also see our breakdown of its ending and our list of the best movies of the year .
items.title_en: Street Fighter Tops the Box Office With $51 Million Opening Weekend Amid Lackluster Reviews

items.title: Quentin Tarantino Says He's 'Written a Script' for 10th and Final Film, But He Wants to 'Live' Before Making It
items.excerpt: Quentin Tarantino has confirmed he's "written a script" for his 10th and final film, but he's going to "live" a little before making it.
items.content_text: Quentin Tarantino has confirmed he's "written a script" for his 10th and final film, but he's going to "live" a little before making it. The Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood and Kill Bill filmmaker teased his plans for his long-in-development finale movie during an appearance on The Graham Norton Show . He said he has a script for a film he "could" do, and it's one he also happens to "really, really like," but he's got a checklist of things to take care of before diving into it. "I've written a script that I could do that I really, really like, but I have to do the play and see who I am, right?" Tarantino said, referencing his upcoming West End play, The Popinjay Cavalier. "I'll finish the play, and then I'll go back, be with my family for a while, and then live and then see what that guy wants to do." The director's words were in response to a question from show host Graham Norton, who asked about his "10th" and "final film." Tarantino didn't skip a beat when conjuring up his reply, suggesting that, yes, the plan is still for his next film to be his last whenever it does eventually hit screens. For reference, The Popinjay Cavalier is set to start previews February 23, 2027, and then open one month later, March 18. That means we've got some waiting to do before Tarantino will begin the "then live" phase of his pre-movie plan. How long it will be before he then decides on a script, begins production, and settles on a release date remains to be seen, but don't expect to hear any significant updates for a while. Tarantino mentioned wanting to finish his career as a movie director at film number 10 a few years before the release of his eighth film, The Hateful Eight , in 2014. As Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood came and went as his ninth project in 2019, his decision to put a cap on his big-screen presence has only become more controversial amongst fans. A filmmaker with a very specific number of trend-setters – including Pulp Fiction , Inglourious Basterds , and Django Unchained – the idea of intentionally ending his time as an artist has been deemed confusing and disappointing. That doesn't seem to have phased Tarantino one bit, and the time it's taken for him to get started on the final project suggests he's not in any rush to get started. Rumors surrounding his enigmatic 10th once had moviegoers expecting him to direct what Simon Pegg called a "bats**t crazy" Star Trek film before the director eventually debunked those alleged plans himself . He was also once said to be making a project called The Movie Critic before it, too, was scrapped . It will be some time before Tarantino directs another movie for theaters, but that doesn't mean an opportunity to see his work on the big screen is too far away. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , a Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood follow-up written by Tarantino and directed by David Fincher , will premiere next month . Photo by Frazer Harrison/Getty Images for Epic Games.

items.title: Dev Behind Russian Roulette Drinking Game Cancels Steam Demo Plans Following AI Copycat Concerns
items.excerpt: The developer behind Russian roulette anime game Drunken Goddess Reflux has canceled its plans for a public Steam demo, citing concerns over potential AI copycats.
items.content_text: The developer behind Russian roulette anime game Drunken Goddess Reflux has canceled its plans for a public Steam demo, citing concerns over potential AI copycats. Alliance Arts and Who You's path to launch has seemingly been mostly bump-free since it was announced back in April. Featuring ghostly pinks and purples and a gameplay premise described as "shot glass Russian roulette with a demon who loves you enough to kill you," the recent reveal that it would launch this December only made its future feel clearer. Part of that release date announcement included the promise that a demo would launch October 19, but as explained in an update post on Steam , those plans have changed. What was originally intended to be a public release for the Drunken Goddess Reflux demo has now been canceled in favor of a "closed play session for a limited number of participants." It's a last-minute move Alliance Arts apologized for, but its concerns related to rapidly advancing AI technology were simply too great to ignore. "We are concerned that, based on the content of the demo, works imitating or replicating this game's presentation and gameplay could be quickly produced using AI or other tools and released ahead of the game's launch," the developers said in their list of concerns. In other words, sending a demo out into the wild could open the door for nefarious individuals to use AI to generate a low-effort clone or copycat experience. For a team hoping for a successful launch in just a few months, someone coming in to steal its thunder could potentially throw a wrench into things. Alliance Arts' fears emerge amid a time when AI is seeping into the gaming industry in ways most may not have ever expected. For example, mods – including mashups of Elden Ring and Super Mario 64 or Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 and Skate – have regularly gone viral on social media in recent weeks. With the controversial technology expanding in new, unforeseen ways every day, it's a risk the Drunken Goddess Reflux weren't willing to take. Another bullet point concern listed in its message detailed restrictions on posting and streaming gameplay videos, but as the team explained, they "are not currently in a position to properly handle and manage those restrictions." With limited resources to keep nearly unrestricted access to a demo in check, Alliance Arts is moving forward with that closed demo. "We will therefore hold online play sessions in a closed environment," the developer added, "open to those who have reviewed and agreed in advance to the participation requirements and the rules on posting and streaming gameplay videos." Players interested in trying the demonic drinking game out were encouraged to join the Discord server presented in the Steam post. Otherwise, Drunken Goddess Reflux is still scheduled to launch on PC via Steam December 8, 2026.
items.title_en: Dev Behind Russian Roulette Drinking Game Cancels Steam Demo Plans Following AI Copycat Concerns

items.title: Battlefield 6 Devs Respond After Players Take Aim at 'Secuty' Typo and Cosmetic With 5 Pistols
items.excerpt: The Battlefield 6 team has responded after players took aim at a few controversial cosmetics added in Season 5.
items.content_text: The Battlefield 6 team has responded after players took aim at a few controversial cosmetics added in Season 5. Battlefield Studios took to its official Discord server to offer background information on two skins that caused a stir with the launch of Battlefield 6 Season 5 this past week (via MP1st ). The full text confirmed at least one of the issues has a fix in the works, while the other will seemingly remain the same. The cosmetics – one with what appeared to be a typo in the word "security" and another featuring infantry sporting a whopping five pistol holsters – were officially added October 13 and almost immediately drew ire from fans . It's that pesky misspelling, which took the shape of the non-existent word "security" on the armband of a McNeil skin, that the developers say will be fixed when Battlefield 6 Season 5 launches in November. Secuty 😭 It's AI #Battlefield6 https://t.co/8DVphghCSU — Battlefield Intel (@BattlefieldInte) October 13, 2026 "You called it out clearly, and we hear your concerns," the message, acknowledging the memes and conversations surrounding the new skins, said. The note continued: "To be completely frank: Items that miss the mark like this do not reflect the quality standards you expect from us, or that we set for ourselves. We take pride in the craft of our world and our gear, and seeing visual oddities slip through is frustrating for everyone. We are currently examining our internal processes and workflows to pinpoint how these issues occurred and to see how we can tighten our quality control process going forward. Thank you for holding us to high standards." It's a quick acknowledgement – and a promise for a quick fix – that should calm some concerns in the community. The communication from BF Studios and EA, however, did not address how exactly the typo happened in the first place or if there is any merit to the new generative AI accusations launched by fans in the aftermath. 💀 BRO IS CARRYING 5 PISTOLS! WHO APPROVED THIS SKIN? 😭 #Battlefield6 https://t.co/b6o94OkV1o — Battlefield Intel (@BattlefieldInte) October 13, 2026 The other cosmetic that caught fans' eyes this week was the Midnight Mirage skin and its incredible five pistol holsters. It…felt like a bit much at the time, and its presence alongside the typo skin didn't do it any favors. Battlefield 6 players have kept the first-person shooter's outfits in the conversation since it launch last October, so mistake or not, an outfit like this was bound to draw some attention. As far as BF Studios is concerned, though, that design was not a mistake at all. "This is an intentional creative concept—a nod to over-the-top action movie tropes where an operative inexplicably has another backup weapon strapped to every spare inch of gear," the message explained. "That said, we understand how this could look unintentional when released alongside other cosmetic anomalies." That's where the conversation surrounding Midnight Mirage seems to end, so don't expect any of those pistols to be dropped anytime soon. The team then signed off promising to keep an eye on community response in the future. "As we continue to try out new ideas to see what interests the community, you help us continue to evolve our cosmetics in Battlefield," they said. "Thank you for your continued feedback and support." Battlefield 6 Season 5 launched last week and, like the seasonal content drops before it, will roll out over three waves. The first is already out and added the Vegas Strip and Area 51 maps, as well as a Dead Space crossover . New map European Casino will then arrive alongside a new event and tools come November 10. December 8 will see the addition of map updates for Blackwell Fields and New Sobek City, with more content and other changes also on the way. IGN gave Battlefield 6 multiplayer an 8/10 review . At the time, we said, "With well-layered action and dynamic destruction, Battlefield 6’s multiplayer hits in all the places where it counts most."

items.title: James Cameron Congratulates Marvel After Avengers: Endgame Beats Avatar at the Box Office Yet Again
items.excerpt: James Cameron celebrated Avengers: Endgame beating Avatar at the box office with another social media post after the two movies traded places yet again.
items.content_text: James Cameron celebrated Avengers: Endgame beating Avatar at the box office with another social media post after the two movies traded places yet again. The director behind the smash-hit sci-fi franchise brought Iron Man to the world of Pandora with an image he shared on Instagram today. The update arrived after Marvel Studios' recent re-release, Avengers: Endgame Encore , managed to bring in enough cash to (re)secure its place as the highest-grossing film of all time. "'You are one of the people,'" the post, accompanied by a picture of Iron Man surrounded by Na'vi, said. "Congratulations to Marvel and the #1 Avengers: Endgame: Encore for bringing moviegoers to the cinemas – Jim Cameron." It's more friendly competition in the movie space that is only the latest update in a race that has seen Avatar and Avengers: Endgame trading titles for years. Marvel originally overtook Avatar's record as the highest-grossing movie in the world when it released in 2019. Cameron shared a similarly congratulatory post at the time but later went on to predict that Avatar would reclaim the throne just a few months later. He was proven right in 2021. As Avatar sequels The Way of Water and Fire and Ash came and went, so too did more Marvel Cinematic Universe movies. As Marvel prepared for the release of its new team-up movie, Avengers: Doomsday , this December, it saw an opportunity to revisit the events of Endgame with new bonus footage , thrusting it into the future by revisiting the past. It was a re-release that proved fruitful for the comic book movie company, with Avengers: Endgame going on to nab a big opening weekend at the box office . Despite a massive drop in its second return weekend in theaters, the film reclaimed its title as the highest-grossing movie ever . Re-releases and original premieres included, the final tally, as shared by Box Office Mojo , puts Marvel and the Russo brothers' Avengers: Endgame in first with $2.938 billion and Cameron's Avatar in second with $2.923 billion. Both movies are within spitting distance of the fabled $3 billion number and still miles ahead of this year's third-place champion, Spider-Man: Brand New Day ($2.513 billion). Whether either of them will ever trade places again remains to be seen. At least in terms of IGN reviews, Avengers: Endgame still came out on top. We gave the Marvel movie a 9.5/10 review at the time of its release in 2019. Cameron's 2009 sci-fi movie earned a 9/10 .
items.title_en: James Cameron Congratulates Marvel After Avengers: Endgame Beats Avatar at the Box Office Yet Again

items.title: Ben Affleck's Batman Movie Would Have Featured Arkham Asylum-Inspired Deathstroke Fight and DCEU Batgirl, Joe Manganiello Reveals
items.excerpt: Joe Manganiello has revealed new plot details about Ben Affleck's canceled Batman movie, including information about an Arkham Asylum-inspired fight with Deathstroke and the DCEU's Batgirl.
items.content_text: Joe Manganiello has revealed new plot details about Ben Affleck's canceled Batman movie, including information about an Arkham Asylum-inspired fight with Deathstroke and the DCEU's Batgirl. The actor, who was cast as Slade Wilson before the comic book movie universe was rebooted with the DCU, talked about his time working with Affleck on the canned project in his new book, Bloodlines: A Memoir. Entertainment Weekly shared excerpts from the book, which said the Batman movie would have been packed with reveals – and even a death – for some of Bruce Wayne's closest allies. Affleck's plan for his standalone Caped Crusader flick would have seen Batman primarily tangling with Deathstroke after the character was first teased in a Justice League end-credits sequence . He described the narrative as "a superhero version of David Fincher's The Game" focused on Deathstroke trying to "dismantle Batman's entire life." This is a plot description Manganiello has shared before , but now we know that the iconic DC villain had it out for Batman because he had been led to believe that he murdered his son. Affleck's Bruce Wayne has been known to take lives in the past, but how involved he would have been with the killing of Slade's son is unclear. It sounds like that wouldn't have stopped Deathstroke from tearing Gotham apart to get revenge. Slade's rampage would have also seen him breaking his way into Bruce's ever-secretive Batcave and even taking his butler, Alfred Pennyworth, hostage. This Alfred likely would have been the one played by Jeremy Irons in movies like Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice and Justice League . Another part that would have probably returned in Affleck's canceled movie is J.K. Simmons' Jim Gordon. According to Manganiello, Deathstroke would have killed the Gotham City Police commissioner at some point during the events of the film. Affleck was never able to put his Batman movie together, but these details suggest the project was planned, at least at one point, to be pretty busy for a standalone superhero outing. Adding to the chaos would have been a new Batgirl, who would have joined Batman for a fight against Deathstroke that would nearly kill them both before they "escape via an aboveground train." Comic book movie watchers will remember that Batgirl never made an appearance in the DCEU – at least not officially. An also-canceled standalone movie focused on the character was once in development with Leslie Grace in the titular role before Warner Bros. made the infamous decision to pull the plug well into production. Set photos and early details for that film had Michael Keaton's Bruce Wayne back in the Batsuit and Simmons back as Gordon, so it's hard to say exactly how it would have fit into the DCEU should it have been released. Whether Grace would have played the character in Affleck's Batman movie is also unclear. For the Affleck movie, Manganiello went as far as to explain the movie's final fight sequence, which he described as a "climactic one-on-one showdown through the streets of Gotham. Affleck apparently told the actor that this particular fight sequence would have been inspired by what Entertainment Weekly described as a "CGI fight sequence from the Batman: Arkham Asylum video game helmed by Tim Miller." The fight scene referenced here might be a well-known moment from the first trailer for Batman: Arkham Origins , which featured a lengthy scrap between Deathstroke and Batman in a snowy shipyard. Considering Affleck's movie was canceled and reworked into what eventually became Robert Pattinson and Matt Reeves' The Batman in 2022, we may never know what the film would have looked like, but Manganiello recalls being hopeful at the time. "It sounded good to me," Manganiello writes. "I told Ben how great I thought his films were, especially The Town, and how I was really looking forward to seeing his Best Picture version of a Batman movie." When the Deathstroke actor told Affleck that writing, directing, producing, and starring in a big-budget DC superhero movie sounded like a lot to handle, the Batman actor reportedly replied, "Yeah, I know…But don’t worry, you’re in good hands. You’re in good hands, man." Although so much about what a standalone Batman movie under Affleck's wing would have looked like remains shrouded in mystery, we've learned quite a bit about the process in recent weeks. Affleck said just days ago that reshoots for Justice League marked the lowest point in his career . Manganiello also spoke more about what it felt like to be cast as Deathstroke and then elaborated on his experience post-cancellation . We'll probably never get a DCEU Batman movie, but there is still plenty more of the Caped Crusader coming to live-action. DC Studios bosses James Gunn and Peter Safran are still working to put together The Brave and the Bold and The Batman Part 2 , for example. Set photos from the latter suggest Pattinson's Batsuit may have some new Arkham Asylum-inspired armor .

items.title: Captain Price Actor Sends Message to Fans as Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Campaign Praise Rolls in
items.excerpt: Barry Sloane, the actor behind Call of Duty's Captain Price, has shared a message with fans as praise for Modern Warfare 4's campaign rolls in.
items.content_text: Barry Sloane, the actor behind Call of Duty's Captain Price, has shared a message with fans as praise for Modern Warfare 4's campaign rolls in. Early reactions to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's story mode have filled social media feeds in the first 24 hours since early access players dived in – and most of them seem to be quite positive. Fans online have called it one of the more "brutal" and "intense" campaigns the series has ever seen, with many going as far as to say it holds its own against classic stories featured in games like the original Modern Warfare 2 and Black Ops. It appears to be a winner for publisher Activision and developer Infinity Ward that critics like, too. While Steam reviews paint a "Very Positive" picture, IGN awarded this year's set of story missions an 8/10 . Our reviewer said the Modern Warfare 4 campaign made them "feel something for the series again," adding that it managed to send the reboot saga series out "on a high note." "The MW4 campaign was a 10/10 for me, they made a good story and ended it," one recent Steam review said . "Damn near almost cried at the end LOL." As reviews continue to trickle in, many have taken the time to praise Sloane's work as Captain Price, specifically. The star behind Activision's most recent incarnation of the Task Force 141 leader took to social media to respond to the "kind words" he's received. "Thank you for all the kind words," he said. "I see them. I read them. And I am grateful." As Infinity Ward sought to end this Modern Warfare storyline with the 2026 Call of Duty game, it should come as no surprise to see that the developers took big swings in its story. With that said, full-on, untagged Modern Warfare 4 campaign spoilers have already started to show up across feeds, too. There's not much Activision can do about that, but Sloane used his message as an opportunity to ask fans to keep unfiltered reactions to themselves, at least for now. "Remember," he continued, "let's allow people to enjoy the game in their own time. No spoilers. Bravo 6 – Dark." Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's campaign is out now for early access players. Its DMZ mode will drop Tuesday, October 20, with the full release set to follow Friday, October 23, for PC, Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S. For a full debrief on the events of the FPS franchise's latest story mode, click here . You can also check out the full breakdown of release times here .

items.title: 7 Crazy Movie Premises That Actually Worked
items.excerpt: Before Whalefall, these crazy movie premises actually worked too.
items.content_text: “A young man is swallowed by a whale while searching for his father’s remains deep in the ocean.” That is the elevator pitch for Whalefall , starring Austin Abrams (Resident Evil) and co-written by Daniel Kraus and director Brian Duffield (No One Will Save You). Set for release on October 16, the film is based on Kraus’ 2023 novel, inspired by a viral video of kayakers seemingly being swallowed by a whale . Whalefall’s central conceit is one writers and directors are challenged by, and often dream of, because it raises the questions: Can I pull this off? And how can I make this work? In other words, the absolutely bonkers premise is fertile ground for real creative risk and opportunity. Read our Whalefall Review Of course, Whalefall isn’t the first or only film to take a big leap. Throughout cinema history, bold filmmakers have swung for the fences and connected. Too many for just one list, in fact. Children of Men, Groundhog Day, Parasite, The Truman Show, Tie Me Up! Tie Me Down!, Spirited Away, The City of Lost Children, The Stepford Wives, Inside Out, Poor Things, Everything Everywhere All at Once, and many more could easily have made this list. The following is a small sample of films that successfully stepped out of standard storytelling boxes. Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb (1964) “Gentlemen, you can’t fight in here! This is the War Room!” Positive that communists are poisoning the “precious bodily fluids” of the American populace, General Jack D. Ripper launches an unauthorized nuclear attack on the U.S.S.R., triggering an increasingly farcical crisis which culminates in a dunce's doomsday, an apocalypse driven by insane idiots and a Nazi. One of cinema’s great political satires, Dr. Strangelove opened in 1964, about a year and a half after the Cuban Missile Crisis, when the world held its breath, wondering if we really were going to self-destruct. Stripping away the reasoned tones that politicians of the day used to discuss nightmare scenarios, Dr. Strangelove captures the powerless fear of a populace, and exposes geopolitics for what it so often is: utterly unhinged and stupid (possibly drunk), and treating mass casualty as if it is a child’s game to win or lose. The film cost $1.8 million to make and earned more than $9 million at the domestic box office . Though it was shut out at the Academy Awards with four nominations and zero wins, it earned several nominations and four wins at the BAFTAs, including Best British Film and Best Film from Any Source. Upon release, reviewers were polarized: some found genius in the dark comedy, while others were disturbed by its treatment of the very real threat of nuclear war. Over time, it has become director Stanley Kubrick’s highest-rated film on Rotten Tomatoes, at 98%, and was deemed so influential that the National Film Registry selected it as one of its first 25 films in 1989. Director Michael Mann went so far as to say he wasn’t really interested in movies until he saw Dr. Strangelove. It remains a standard-bearer for satire. It captures essential truth, if not (necessarily) objective reality. As for reality, military officials criticized the film upon release, yet, coincidentally or not, made internal changes that mapped to the vulnerabilities Dr. Strangelove exposed . Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) In a world where sentient cartoons live alongside humans, Eddie Valiant – an alcoholic private detective with a vendetta against toons – is hired to investigate a sultry cartoon femme fatale, Jessica Rabbit, who may be cuckolding her stuttering rabbit husband, Roger. When her alleged lover is found dead, Valiant is forced to protect the unruly rabbit and drawn into a sinister toon conspiracy. Roger Rabbit was a hit with audiences and critics alike right out of the gate, and stands at 96% on Rotten Tomatoes. Praised for its visionary storytelling, which mixes zany cartoon comedy with classic noir tropes, and for its revolutionary technical achievement, the film left viewers spellbound. Though live action and animation had been integrated before, audiences had never seen anything quite like Roger Rabbit. Bob Hoskins’ emotional performance as the detective on a redemption arc was lauded, particularly in that he was acting, essentially, with empty space for much of the film. Kathleen Turner’s rich voice cemented Jessica Rabbit as an iconic animated character. Made for $50 million ($70 million by some estimates ), the film earned just over $350 million worldwide. It had six Academy Award nominations and three wins (plus a Special Achievement Academy Award for animation direction) and was added to the National Film Registry in 2016 . Thanks to executive producer Steven Spielberg’s negotiations, it wowed audiences by bringing together animated characters from both Warner Bros. and Disney. Along with The Little Mermaid, it also helped usher in the Disney Animation renaissance. Similar releases followed, including 1992’s Cool World, starring Brad Pitt as a human detective and Kim Basinger as a cartoon femme fatale named Holli Would, and 1996’s Space Jam, which teamed Michael Jordan with the Looney Tunes. Arguably, the film that’s come closest to capturing Roger Rabbit’s appeal is the recent Coyote vs. Acme, but, for many, nothing truly touches the 1988 classic. According to director Robert Zemeckis , Stanley Kubrick deeply appreciated the film and, while watching it, searched for the hidden “sleight of hand” movie magic that made it all come together, before ultimately realizing it was “just an incredible amount of backbreaking work” that made Roger Rabbit possible. It’s a Wonderful Life (1946) A suicidal man embittered by career sacrifices and disappointments, and facing ruin and jail, meets with a fledgling angel (eager to advance in his own vocation) on Christmas Eve. In order for the latter to win the promotion he wants (get his wings), he must convince the former that there’s more to life than work and material success, and that his impact on the world has been sizable and good, despite all evidence to the contrary. Perhaps that’s a hyperbolic synopsis, but the fact is, while director Frank Capra’s holiday favorite may be considered a sentimental classic today, audiences at the time of its release seemingly weren’t ready for this unorthodox take on Christmas cheer. Though it received mixed to somewhat positive reviews (particularly praising Jimmy Stewart’s lead performance) and ultimately earned five Oscar nominations, it won no Academy Awards beyond a Technical Achievement Award and was a box-office flop. RKO, the studio that released the film, reported a $525,000 loss . But It’s a Wonderful Life did nearly gain notoriety – via controversy , when the FBI flagged it to the House Un-American Activities Committee (which was investigating potential Communist influences in Hollywood), noting anti-capitalist undertones (as the film’s banker was the most hated character). Alas, it couldn’t even get negative PR, as the committee decided not to bring the creators in to testify. The film was largely overlooked in the decades that followed. Capra himself was taken aback , if pleasantly so, when it finally found its audience. The full story is more complex, but, effectively, a clerical fluke meant the film’s copyright lapsed in 1974 , making it cheap to run on television during the holidays, which it did for many years. The copyright situation was eventually resolved through the rights in the underlying story and music. By then, it had become a beloved standard. Distance gave viewers space to see what was always there. Audiences and critics alike recognized the special magic in the strange mix of sentimentality, whimsy, very real and deeply painful human despair, and the essential truth that we all desire to know, truly know, that our lives matter. In a 1999 essay, film critic Roger Ebert said this film belonged to a category that could withstand indefinite viewings: “Like great music, they improve with familiarity.” Years after it opened and flopped, It’s a Wonderful Life became a holiday television staple, drawing millions of viewers for its Christmas Eve broadcasts, and now holds a 94% rating on Rotten Tomatoes. Being John Malkovich (1999) While working a bland office job, struggling street puppeteer Craig Schwartz stumbles upon a portal to actor John Malkovich’s mind, where he can experience the celebrity’s life for exactly 15 minutes before being spat back out onto the New Jersey Turnpike. He and the co-worker he’s in love with start a business charging $200 per person for a visit into the actor’s experience. Eventually, multiple characters battle to permanently take over Malkovich’s life, creating a series of betrayals, identity crises, opportunities found and then lost, and the annihilation of the self. Charlie Kaufman’s surreal screenplay is arguably one of the biggest swings on this list. Malkovich himself initially worried it would bomb , and the script circulated Hollywood with no takers. One exec reportedly asked, “Why the f— can’t it be Being Tom Cruise?” However, director Francis Ford Coppola got the script to his daughter’s then-boyfriend, Spike Jonze, who directed it and helped get it produced. The movie opened to great acclaim, presumably stunning skeptical industry players. It has a 94% on Rotten Tomatoes, with Roger Ebert calling it “endlessly inventive,” adding that “[it] has ideas enough for half a dozen films.” Critics celebrated its inventiveness, layered themes, and ensemble performances from John Cusack, Cameron Diaz, Catherine Keener, and, of course, John Malkovich. It cost $13 million to produce and went on to earn either $23 million or $32 million globally (depending on the source). It didn’t win any of its three Oscar nominations, but it won Best First Feature and Best First Screenplay at the Independent Spirit Awards. It appears on multiple “best of” lists, including Empire magazine ’s 500 Greatest Movies of All Time and the Writers Guild of America’s 101 Greatest Screenplays Ever Written . Like Kaufman’s other films (two of which, Adaptation and Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, nearly made this list), Being John Malkovich demonstrates what is possible when you follow even the most nonsensical threads of imagination. The Raid: Redemption (2011) A SWAT team, trapped in a hostile high-rise, must battle its way up the stairs to capture a crime lord; end of story. The Raid is unique on this list in that the plot isn’t a fit of wild imagination; rather, it has almost no plot at all. It has a premise and wall-to-wall unparalleled fight sequences. It grips the viewer and doesn’t let go for the entire runtime, leaving audiences breathless and feeling like they, too, just punched their way to victory. It’s exhilarating, near-perfect action that other films have chased for 15 years. The Indonesian actioner cost $1.1 million to make, according to director Gareth Evans , and earned over $9 million worldwide at the box office, plus another $10 million in U.S. DVD and Blu-ray sales alone. No traditional narrative necessary. It stands at 87% on Rotten Tomatoes and performed well during its film festival run – Evans said he was “blown away” by the reception at the Toronto International Film Festival. The movie became an industry reference point, with John Wick director Chad Stahelski telling Den of Geek that directors unfamiliar with fight choreography would specifically ask for something like The Raid, among other iconic action films. Yayan Ruhian and Cecep Arif Rahman, two actors from The Raid franchise, were ultimately cast as two of Keanu Reeves’ adversaries in John Wick: Chapter 3 – Parabellum. The film is a beloved fan favorite and cultural touchstone for best-in-class hand-to-hand action. Get Out (2017) On a trip to visit his girlfriend’s parents, a talented photographer makes a horrific discovery: a group of Obama-voting white suburbanites has found a way to use misophonia-inducing teaspoons, hypnosis, and surgery to transplant the consciousness of wealthy, older white people into young, Black kidnappees, whose own psyches are sent into a purgatorial “sunken place.” Director Jordan Peele’s groundbreaking debut became an instant cultural phenomenon, blending social commentary with genuinely entertaining horror. The director builds real suspense, psychological terror, and tension-releasing humor into a film that lays systemic racism bare through a deeply imaginative metaphor. It has a 98% on Rotten Tomatoes, and Peele made Academy Awards history as the first Black writer to win an Oscar for Best Original Screenplay. Get Out was also nominated for Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Actor (Daniel Kaluuya). In late 2021, the WGA named the script the #1 Greatest Screenplay of the 21st Century (So Far). Financially, Get Out was a juggernaut, making $255 million worldwide on a $4.5 million budget, and breaking The Blair Witch Project’s domestic record as the highest-grossing debut film based on an original screenplay. Director Christopher Nolan had this to say of Get Out: “How often do you get the experience of seeing something that you have no idea where it's going to go, and then it goes somewhere far more interesting than you ever imagined?" Barbie (2023) Faced with an unexpected existential crisis, Barbie must travel from the utopia of Barbieland into the “real” world to find and soothe the unhappy person playing with her so that she can once again experience the sweet oblivion of not thinking about death, or life, or meaning… and bask in thighs free of cellulite. Ken tags along and, upon discovering patriarchy, starts an uprising when he returns to Barbieland. The overall sentiment when Barbie debuted was that this movie absolutely should not work . Yet it surprised and delighted audiences with its mix of subversive humor (that both acknowledges and reframes Barbie’s cultural impact), standout performances from producer and star Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling (as Barbie and Ken), and an optimistic core. It inspired multiple viewings for many audience members, some of whom came to theaters decked out in celebratory pink. Doctor Strange director Scott Derrickson said the film was one of his two favorites that year, and an example of IP “treated with true brilliance,” calling it an “extraordinary movie on every level.” Set against Oppenheimer in the summer’s race for dominance, affectionately known as Barbenheimer, the film catapulted to box office success. It was a risk for both Mattel and Warner Bros., who distributed it. They trusted co-writer and largely indie director Greta Gerwig, who’d never helmed a film this big, with an iconic but controversial doll and a $128 million budget. The bet paid off: Barbie earned a staggering $1.4 billion worldwide at the box office , holds an 88% on Rotten Tomatoes, and received eight Oscar nominations, winning Best Original Song for “What Was I Made For?” and taking home the first-ever Golden Globe for Cinematic and Box Office Achievement. Ultimately, the film’s pathos stayed with viewers. Barbie is the picture of stagnant perfection, so who better to take a messy journey where triumph lies in living the most mundane moments of a human life? What are your favorite crazy movie premises that somehow worked? Let’s discuss in the comments!
items.title_en: 7 Crazy Movie Premises That Actually Worked

items.title: We Sat Down with D&D Game Designer James Wyatt to Talk Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft
items.excerpt: At New York Comic Con, I got a chance to sit down with Wizards of the Coast Principal Game Designer James Wyatt to talk about the first Universes Beyond expansion for D&D.
items.content_text: Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft is less than a month away, and it already looks like it's going to be a massive expansion to the tabletop game. But there are still a lot of questions about whether this new expansion is going to lean more towards the combat-oriented approach of the MMO or just be a traditional D&D game on Azeroth. At New York Comic Con, I got a chance to sit down with Wizards of the Coast principal game designer James Wyatt to talk about the first Universes Beyond expansion for D&D. From how he was talking about the expansion, it really does sound more like a D&D game taking place on Azeroth than trying to shove WoW's complicated mechanics and combat focus on the TTRPG. IGN: I know that there are a lot of people who play both WoW and D&D, and I've heard some WoW players say that this is going to get them into D&D. Does the Expansion have a good on-ramp for those players? James Wyatt: That is not its purpose, but I think it is a fantastic on-ramp in terms of someone who's a WoW player. Sitting down to make a D&D character, you're like, "Okay, what's a Tiefling? What's a Dragonborn? And what do these classes mean?" Whereas if you have that foundation of here's the WoW species, here's the WoW classes, you know the kind of character you want to make right away. This can help you steer and make those choices as a new player. We also have a very brief introductory "What is D&D?" just in case you don't know or for people who aren't familiar with it. And we steer you to D&D Beyond in particular as a place to find resources to help you get started. So yeah, we took this down for a playtest at Blizzard last fall in the early stages, and Blizzard employees who had signed up, they signed up blind for a playtest of something. They didn't know what. And so some of them were like, "Woo, D&D. Yes, I love D&D." And others are like, "Okay, I've never played it before. How does this go?" And I always love playing with new players because they don't know what they're supposed to do. So they are more willing to try anything they can imagine, which to my mind is really what the game is all about. I was just telling the story of the guy who was playing the Forsaken Warlock who decided that, because he had no lower jaw, he couldn't properly cast spells. So his first spell backfired and knocked him down the stairs. And so then he tore off his own arm and threw it at the monster. And, awesome! That's Dungeons & Dragons in a nutshell. It's not "What buttons do I have to press?" It's "What can I imagine and how do I do that? What does it look like?" IGN: Yeah. Speaking of the combat, I know that there's a selection of dungeons that have been poured into the game, but obviously there are just too many dungeons in World of Warcraft to bring all of them over. So why did you pick the dungeons that you picked? Wyatt: There were a couple of factors that went into that. One of them is that we started with this section on conflicts of Azeroth, which outlines the six conflicts that really have been the driving forces behind most of the expansions of WoW and talk about how they shape the world, and how you might bring them into a campaign. All of the dungeons, I think, tie into these themes. That was one of the things that we used as a selection criteria is, does it reflect the themes of the conflicts that we're trying to emphasize here? So that was one. I was looking at popularity ranking on some wiki as another factor, just trying to get at what Dungeons people love and what's resonant for them. We started with a much larger list, made it smaller. So then it was what can we do in the space that we have and what works for the various level ranges of characters and that sort of thing. IGN: There are some people who are probably going to want to see more of the raids. I think the only raid that I saw on the list was Onyxia's Lair, I might be mistaken. But will people be able to create their own Icecrown Citadel? Wyatt: Icecrown Citadel, we are doing as a digital download adventure. We have a separate map pack that has five double-sided poster maps that are the boss fights from Icecrown Citadel. And that comes with a code for a digital download of the Icecrown Citadel adventure. So you can play through that. But I ran Blackfathom Deeps 20 years ago. It was just downloading the map from the internet and making up stats for Nagas at the time. And so using the tools in this book, you can absolutely adapt any dungeon you want to. IGN: I saw some people concerned that this will be too focused on combat and having prescriptive dungeons. What would you say to that? Wyatt: I think that's kind of the opposite of what we were going for, because the beauty of D&D is that when you walk into Shadowfang Keep, you can talk to anybody you meet, you can interact with anything you can see. And so the possibilities just open up tremendously over what a developer can program into any game, no matter how much care they're putting into it, because you have a DM at the table who can improvise and decide what happens. So the dungeons that are presented here are given a pretty light touch and it's sort of like, okay, here's the dungeon map, here's the pins in the map that mark the bosses that we know you're going to encounter at some point. And what happens in between is largely a matter of improv and that you can roll on tables to generate encounters if you want a combat encounter, but you can also do something where you're exploring the environment in a way that you can't necessarily do in the MMO. IGN: I take it that even the adventure hooks that you have open on that page there of Dire Maul, I'm sure people can create their own adventure hooks and assign their own reputation rewards and everything like that. Wyatt: Yeah. IGN: So this is for people who are familiar with Dungeons & Dragons at large. This is more of a guideline of how to play a game within World of Warcraft than anything else. Wyatt: Yes, exactly. It is a great big toolbox. I mean, that's how I describe most of the books that I work on. I don't write a lot of adventure products. I do a lot of source books, and really there's that sense of we've got character options, we've got monsters, we've got dungeons you can explore. We've got guidelines for crafting your own campaign, and we've got just a big blank slate for you to play with. IGN: World of Warcraft's obviously an evolving game that never really sits in one place. This goes up to the beginning of Midnight. Obviously, there's going to be more stories that come out over time. Are there going to be supplemental products or will it just be like, we gave you the tools, you know the story, kind of do your own thing with it? Wyatt: Who knows? Okay, I keep saying that if I get to do another World of Warcraft book, I might postpone my retirement a little bit in order to work on it because I had so much fun working on this, loved it so much. And that depends entirely on my relationship with Blizzard and how things go from here, but I would love to do more. And honestly, the book doesn't spend as much time on the War Within and Midnight as it could have. There's almost nothing about Xal'atath in here. Would've loved to give her a stat block, but she didn't sort of make the cut. And I'm not sure we could give her a stat block. IGN: She does play into that Old Gods and the Void conflict pretty heavily. Wyatt: Yeah. There's absolutely more we can do even with the story that exists now, as well as future stories. And I'm keeping a list that will be my outline as soon as I get the go-ahead and start working in another book if that ever happens. But for now, absolutely, if those are the next expansion is all about, give me something that they might focus on. IGN: The next expansion is going to be The Last Titan, so I assume it's going to be about the Titans. Wyatt: Right. Well, we can tell you a little bit about the Titans in here somewhere, beginning of chapter five. And honestly, my expectation is that anybody using this book is also going to spend a lot of time on the wikis because that information is there. So yeah, we've got lots of resources for making a character that probably is not going to change significantly. I mean, the next time they give us a new class, it would be fun to do that in another D&D book. IGN: Tell me a little bit about working the Devourer Demon Hunter into the book. Wyatt: Pretty much as soon as I got access to the Midnight beta, I went and made a Devourer and started playing around with it and was reading what was, again, on the wikis about it. And so we already had the Demon Hunter set up with Havoc and Vengeance and just added some more spells and some direction about how to steer your Demon Hunter in that spec. They've got their own column of spells here with all the consuming soul stuff. IGN: How did you work the WoW classes into D&D without kind of putting a wrench in the way classes traditionally work in Dungeons & Dragons? Wyatt: The word I keep using is, rather than translation, paraphrase, that for each class I sat down and I looked at their abilities and their talent trees and all the things they can do. And I sort of cut off around level 60, I think. I don't remember now. I'd have to look at my spreadsheets. I have spreadsheets. Nobody told me that being a writer was going to involve so many spreadsheets. And I looked for things that are already in D&D that we want to make sure to highlight in that specialization and that class, and look for opportunities to create new spells or feats or battle master maneuvers, or anything else to help evoke the most iconic flavor things. Talents are really fiddly in WoW and D&D mechanics are not that fiddly. We don't deal with math at such a granular scale. And so again, evoking the flavor is more important to us than reproducing the mechanics in any way. So each specialization has a selection of feats that would be good to help you do that. There is a fundamental difference though, that if you're playing a healing spec Paladin, you are a healer as opposed to a tank spec Paladin, who is a tank. And in D&D, no matter what Paladin and subclass you choose and what feat you choose, you're both, you're a healer and a tank. And so you're not as narrowly defined by your role. So that remains true. And if you're playing a Priest, you can be wearing more than cloth armor because we couldn't easily take something away from the Cleric class to fit, and you're still casting the spells that you expect a WoW Priest to be casting. So all of the classes I think are a little broader and give you more range of options while still helping you focus in on the role you're supposed to be playing. IGN: I feel like in WoW stories, characters that embody those classes follow those rules anyways where it's more broad. Wyatt: Yeah. They keep saying Anduin is a priest and there he is in plate armor with his sword. IGN: Yeah, he is a special Priest, isn't he? So what about the mechanics for bosses? I know you described the Litch King Arthas fight, and I progressed that fight when it was current on Heroic 25, and it was hell, with mechanics like defile where you stand in it and it gets bigger. Is it as fraught or as dangerous, or is there kind of... Wyatt: I mean, he's challenge rating 25, where D&D characters go up to level 20. So you know, it's going to be a tough fight. It's different because D&D combats are shorter in terms of the number of things you or the boss can do in the fight because they often take long enough even at three or four rounds compared to how quickly an MMO raid battle plays out, relatively speaking. So again, that idea of paraphrase rather than translation, we're trying to evoke the feeling of that fight without reproducing it exactly. But there's a lot going on here that will feel very familiar. IGN: Could you go in and talk Arthas out of invading Azeroth with the Scourge or sneak in and steal the Helm of Domination and put it on yourself? Wyatt: Theoretically. You can certainly try. And that's again the beauty of it, that you can talk to anybody. IGN: Can you tell me a little bit more about the reputation system? Why did you think that was such an important thing to work into a Warcraft tabletop game? Wyatt: So the renown system in the Dungeon Masters guide is sort of an optional rule. It's not something that we spend a lot of time with in the base game, but it is a great tool for giving factions in the world some kind of heft, a significant impact on characters' lives. And so given particularly the importance of the Alliance and the Horde, and also the other factions in the game, I thought it would be pretty cool to use the renown system to reflect, to give characters some investment in those factions. But fundamentally, you start caring about the welfare of the Horde if you're fighting for the Horde, and you're getting renown with the Horde, and you're getting benefits for that devotion to them. So it's not load bearing. You can ignore it if you want to. The campaign that I'm playing in right now, it's weird because we've time traveled. We've gone back from Midnight to Classic. And so I'm not sure any of us are fully rooted in the world yet, but I'm really curious to see how that plays out over time. I think we might have just gotten a renown reward in our last adventure, but I can't remember for sure. So yeah, it's fun. It's a way to root characters in the world and it's not essential. In the Icecrown Citadel adventure, we do a whole separate thing for your Renown with the Ashen Verdict, which goes up more quickly than you might expect Renown to go up in the core book. But then you can get your rings improved by Armis the Penitent as your renown increases, and you're also collecting things that can make Shadowmourne and doing all of that in the context of working through the raid once rather than working through it repeatedly. IGN: I think that's where the friction in my head is at. Because of all the time I've spent in WoW, I associate reputation with these massive grinds. Wyatt: Yeah. That really is the key difference that even in Icecrown Citadel, I planned it out so that you get to, I think you get to 50 just about the time you kill the Lich King. But it's like every single encounter in the Citadel, your renown increases by one or two, which is bigger than the rate we expect for most of these factions. The general idea is, and in the DMG, we even give you a conversion. If you don't want to track renown points, you can just use character level so that by the time you're 17th level, we assume you're exalted with your home faction. IGN: On the time travel thing you mentioned earlier, the Chromie time. So for me, in the actual video game World of Warcraft, Chromie Time always felt kind of shoehorned in as "we need to get you to end game as fast as possible." And Chromie Time was just kind of the method to do that. Why Chromie Time? Wyatt: Well, two things going on. The first is that Chromie wrote a little introduction to the book. IGN: I love that. Wyatt: Me too. Thank you. Where she's basically saying, "I put this book together to let you visit whatever part, basically to give you your own timeline to play in." It's a way of expressly giving the reader permission to ignore Canon, fundamentally. That's all it is. The specific example of the campaign I'm playing in, that's our DM's concoction of, okay, the campaign I want to run is modern characters. We started off in Silvermoon City. We've just repelled Xal'atath. We're eight characters. We've just helped support the effort to repel Xal'atath. And then suddenly the time stream changes and we're in a Silvermoon city that is run by dragons. And what has happened? So we fight some dragons and get to safety and meet Chromie who says the time stream's gone amuck. I've got to send you back 20 years to before this to prevent whatever the Infinite Dragonflight has done to mess up the timestream. So that's the story we're playing, not essential to what's in the book. IGN: Okay. So it's not some scheme for Chromie to become the Bronze Aspect? Wyatt: Who knows? Maybe in your campaign. IGN: She deserves it. Wyatt: It's true. She's also got little notes scattered throughout the book. IGN: Oh yeah? Wyatt: Not very many of them, but wherever we had space on a page, she wrote a little note. "All these King Gorducks, or is it King Gordock? Anyway, I think all Big Ogres would benefit from spending some time small." IGN: I think they would. That's a great addition. My final question is about Forever. I know you mentioned that it came out too late to get added to the book in any meaningful way, but if somebody wanted to add the Skyborne race or add the new zones that were added in, which I think a lot of the new zones in Forever were kind of cut content that existed in vanilla anyways, like Mount Hyjal. Wyatt: Right. Yeah. I remember seeing that big blank spot on the map because I was playing early on. Yeah. Adding a new Elven lineage is not super complicated. It might be fun for us to talk to Blizzard about maybe doing that in a D&D Beyond drop or something. But anything else that they've added content-wise, I think the content that they're adding is very easy to just port into the D&D campaign you're playing. And again, you can do anything you want. You can go anywhere you want. IGN: I have to ask: Would you rather play Forever or Retail? Wyatt: I wish I had time to do both. Right now I really don't have time to do either. So I've been dabbling with forever just a little bit, but I'm anxious to... I haven't finished the Midnight storyline yet, I think. So I'm anxious to get back to that, too.

items.title: The Street Fighter Movie Makes a Mistake Mortal Kombat Already Learned From
items.excerpt: Why are fighting game movies so scared of fighting tournaments? The Street Fighter movie is just the latest example.
items.content_text: Spoilers follow for Street Fighter. Put on your gis and gloves, fighting fans, because Street Fighter is now in theaters. The latest attempt to adapt the venerated fighting game franchise for the big screen may not be getting off to the best start with critics, but fans of the series will likely go check it out for themselves. The film does have its positive aspects, such as the gorgeous 2D animation used for flashback sequences as well as plenty of easter eggs and fighting moves ripped right from the classic games. But as a whole, Street Fighter is too slapdash to be a fully satisfying cinematic experience, and one of the biggest reasons why is that the film doesn’t use the seemingly obvious way to structure itself. Street Fighter is a game about a fighting tournament, and while there is technically a tournament in the film, it isn’t the main focus. In fact, the movie goes out of its way to make the tournament feel like a largely incidental part of the plot, and this hurts the movie in more ways than one. What makes this even more bizarre is that this is a mistake that Mortal Kombat already made in the 2021 reboot, but the filmmakers behind Street Fighter didn’t learn the lesson from their fellow fighting franchise. How did this happen? Let’s take a look. World of Warriors Street Fighter may be the first movie in this new continuity, but it takes its cast and premise from the second game, Street Fighter II. This is a smart move, since not only is Street Fighter II the most famous game in the franchise, but the first entry is commonly considered to be a well-meaning prototype for a series that didn’t fully come together until the sequel. The movie doesn’t erase the first game though, instead incorporating the first World Warrior tournament and Ryu’s victory over Muay Thai master Sagat into the animated pre-title sequence to give us backstory for our main characters, Ryu and Ken Masters. The main plot picks up six years later when main villain M. Bison sets up a second World Warrior tournament in the hopes of enticing Ryu into the spotlight to defend his title so that Bison can steal Ryu’s Hado power — that’s the energy that powers his famous Hadoken move from the games. More Street Fighting! Street Fighter Review Street Fighter: How Can There Be an Ending Explained When There Is No Ending? The tournament draws in many notable fighters from around the world, and while you would think the tournament would take up a big chunk of the runtime, it really doesn’t. Bison puts up only a cursory front of interest in the tournament, immediately kidnapping Ryu and absconding to his lab to work on draining Ryu’s Hado power. Ken wants to become the champion to prove himself to his deceased master Gouken, but his efforts to win the tournament only make up about half of his story. Ryu doesn’t participate at all on account of being kidnapped before it starts, even though he goes through the trouble of defeating E. Honda ahead of time to take his spot in the roster. Nor does Chun-Li, who — egregiously for the film — was the only woman who competed in the game. While nearly every Street Fighter II character is present in some capacity, the film moves many of the major players to the margins of the actual tournament. This results in a bewildering viewing experience where the tournament “begins” in the second act by jumping in after one of the fights is already over, with Guile having been eliminated off-screen by Vega. Some of the other fights are similarly skipped, and multiple rounds are decided by forfeit because a character is off doing something else for plot reasons. This makes the tournament such an afterthought that it becomes impossible to invest in the scenes that do take place during it, since it’s clear that the tournament is not a priority. It also means that we never see multiple fan favorite characters like Guile and Zangief in action aside from a pointless scene early on where a bunch of the contenders brawl in a nightclub. It’s disappointing not just because we don’t get enough fighting in our Street Fighter movie, but because the filmmakers should have known better when Mortal Kombat already suffered from this same narrative stumble. Missing Kombat I know it may seem like we’ve all lived several lives since the ancient times of 2021, but that was when the first of the Mortal Kombat reboot films was released. Although it did well enough financially to secure a sequel, the film was a mess on the creative side, feeling like one of the worst examples of focusing on all the wrong things when trying to launch a new franchise. Instead of an engaging story centered around beloved characters from the games participating in a fighting tournament starring champions from different realms, Mortal Kombat tried and failed to endear fans to series newcomer Cole Young and never actually featured the eponymous Mortal Kombat tournament. In fact, the villain Shang Tsung’s plan is to prevent the tournament from taking place by killing Earthrealm’s champions before it can happen. It’s a strange gambit that feels like it’s working backwards to do something different instead of just delivering on straightforward genre expectations. Given how important the Mortal Kombat tournament is to the series mythology, the film couldn’t help but make me and many others feel like Ian Malcolm in Jurassic Park: “You do plan on having Mortal Kombat in your Mortal Kombat movie, right?” It didn’t work, and much of the fan backlash to the reboot had to do with the movie excising the tournament and making unwelcome changes to MK lore, like the infamous “Arcana” tattoos that provided champions with special powers. It’s no surprise that the much more warmly received Mortal Kombat II not only jettisoned the Arcana concept and brought in series icons like Kitana and Johnny Cage, but also made the tournament the backbone of the story. Sure, the movie may not have set the world on fire, but it was a step in the right direction for a property that hasn’t had the best luck when it comes to adaptations. So it's all the more baffling that Street Fighter falls into such a similar trap. It’s not like the movie sets the tournament aside to fill the runtime with something really interesting or subversive; it’s just thin characters and generic action scenes hastily assembled in a way that struggles to suggest any weight or gravitas. Not that Street Fighter has ever been Shakespeare (although Raul Julia certainly treated it as such in the 1994 film), but the games have enough iconic personalities and cultural pedigree that there’s no reason you can’t deliver a movie with entertaining action and a functional dramatic engine, especially when a conventional tournament provides the perfect built-in narrative structure of a sports movie building up to a climactic showdown. And for all the chatter about Bison’s plans to harness Psycho Power, we don’t see him go toe-to-toe with Ryu. Not that Street Fighter has ever been Shakespeare, but there's no reason you can't deliver a movie with entertaining action and a functional dramatic engine. Instead, Street Fighter awkwardly jams in a battle between Ryu and Akuma as its climax while shuffling Bison, who has been the antagonist for most of the film, off to make a hasty getaway for a presumed sequel. And yes, Akuma is foreshadowed as Ryu’s rival via flashbacks, and it’s said beforehand he will challenge the winner of the tournament, but that rings a bit hollow when Ryu doesn’t actually win said tournament. Back to Basics Street Fighter feeling half-formed is especially disappointing because video game adaptations are having a major moment. Between the Sonic the Hedgehog films becoming smash hits, acclaimed shows based on Fallout and Castlevania, and Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil movie garnering critical praise and the biggest box office take in the series’ history, the video game curse has most certainly been broken. Even Mortal Kombat has risen from the ashes with the aforementioned Mortal Kombat II being a solid and entertaining entry. Street Fighter had all the ingredients to continue the trend, but instead places fan references and sequel teases ahead of meat and potatoes storytelling. It all leads to a weird non-ending with the heroes in a car chasing after M. Bison, who has since recruited Sagat to his cause. This sequel setup would be far less frustrating if it felt like much of consequence happened in this movie. I say this as someone with a lot of love for the offbeat fantasy lore of games like Soulcalibur and Mortal Kombat: Most people do not play fighting games for their world-building. They want to see their favorite characters in exciting 1v1 action, and the tournament conceit provides the most sensible framework to deliver that. That’s not to say you should skimp on trying to tell an actual story with the characters involved, but structurally, can we just start with the fundamentals? We’ll see if Street Fighter does well enough to warrant another round, but if it does, it would be better for everyone if the filmmakers remembered what made this franchise popular in the first place. items.title: Red Rising Greenlit for Movie Adaptation With Author Pierce Brown to Produce
items.excerpt: The Red Rising book series by author Pierce Brown has officially been greenlit for a movie adaptation from Paramount Pictures, with Hunger Games alum Francis Lawrence to direct.
items.content_text: The Red Rising book series by author Pierce Brown has officially been greenlit for a movie adaptation from Paramount Pictures, with Hunger Games alum Francis Lawrence to direct. Red Rising is getting the Hollywood treatment more than a decade after it was first published in 2014. As confirmed by The Hollywood Reporter on October 16, Paramount Pictures has picked up the rights to the series, which will be brought to the screen by director Francis Lawrence. Lawrence is known for his work on another young adult screen adaptation in the Hunger Games series, having directed every movie in the franchise sans the first one, which was directed by Gary Ross. Lawrence recently directed Stephen King adaptation The Long Walk , as well as the forthcoming Sunrise on the Reaping , the latest movie in the Hunger Games franchise. Lawrence is also set to produce the Red Rising film alongside Cameron MacConomy for their about:blank production company, as well as Francesco Goedhuis and the author of the Red Rising saga himself, Pierce Brown. Brown reacted to the news in a post on his Instagram account , writing, "Let fall the iron rain. Bloodydamn, I love this team." Joining Red Rising is Justin Rhodes, who will write the movie’s script. Eagle-eyed IGN readers will recognize this name, as he is also involved in Netflix’s live-action Bioshock movie , which is reportedly still in early development. Rhodes is known for films like Terminator: Dark Fate, Traveler, and Liminal. Red Rising is a sprawling book series that is planned to end with its seventh and final installment, which as yet has no release date. Set in a galaxy with a strict, color-coded caste system, the books follow Darrow, a Red — the lowest rank on the social totem pole. He and his fellow Reds toil tirelessly in the mines of Mars, with the hope that one day, they will be able to make the planet habitable for human life… but it turns out that this was already accomplished generations ago. After learning of this massive betrayal, Darrow makes it his mission to infiltrate the highest social caste, the Golds, and set things right across the entire galaxy in a deadly conflict that spans more than a decade. If you're interested in getting into the books, you can check out our guide to navigating this sprawling adventure , which will no doubt come in handy once the movie eventually gets released. This is the latest exciting news for book readers after Prime Video’s Fourth Wing series found its Xaden and Violet in actors Emilio Sakraya and Esther McGregor.
